summary: BBN suggests adding a restart procedure to the File Transfer Protocol. Remote job service sites commonly handle very long files, such as hundreds of pages of printer output, so a failed transfer should be able to resume near where it stopped instead of starting over.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC proposes a way to resume a long file transfer after a connection failure. The user and server use sequence numbers to agree where sending should continue.

questions: how can file transfers resume on the arpanet
why did large files need restart capability
how do sequence numbers help recover broken transfers
subtitle: A proposal to let FTP resume a long file transfer after a connection breaks.

tldr.problem: A long file transfer could fail after a large amount of data had moved, forcing users to start the transfer again.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal adds four FTP commands that use sequence numbers to agree on a restart point or to suggest another point the server can locate.
tldr.outcome: The RFC asks the Network Working Group to consider adding restart support to FTP and invites comments or counter-proposals.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 281 as Unknown and records that it updates RFC 265. The text presents a suggested FTP addition and does not state whether it was adopted.

sections.title: Why Transfers Need a Restart
sections.content:
The RFC grew from discussion about using FTP for Remote Job Service. The author notes that some files, such as printer output, can be hundreds of pages long, so restarting from the beginning after a path failure wastes transferred data.

A restart procedure needs both ends to agree exactly where the resumed transmission should begin.
sections.plainLanguage: Large files can take a long time to send. If the path breaks near the end, a restart feature could avoid sending the earlier part again.

sections.title: Choosing a Restart Marker
sections.content:
The underlying Data Transfer Protocol offers information separators and sequence numbers as possible markers. After discussion, the authors favor sequence numbers because separators in transparent block mode may not identify a restart location unambiguously.

The proposal notes that this choice would not help hosts that do not use sequence numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides need a marker they can identify in the old and resumed transfer. The proposal uses sequence numbers for that marker.

sections.title: The Proposed FTP Commands
sections.content:
The four proposed commands are Append at sequence number, Retrieve at sequence number, Resume Retrieve, and Use the sequence number. The first two let a user request a particular restart point, while Resume Retrieve lets the server choose one.

If the requested point cannot be found, the server can refuse or suggest a sequence number it can locate. The sender can then accept that point or abandon the restart.
sections.plainLanguage: The user can ask for a specific restart point or let the server choose one. If the server suggests a different point, the user can accept or stop.
